sentence: The shoulder is built from the clavicle and scapula, which together form the shoulder (pectoral) girdle, and the top of the humerus, which meets the scapula at the shoulder joint.
evidence: Clavicle + scapula = shoulder (pectoral) girdle is standard anatomy. StatPearls Shoulder describes the shoulder girdle linking the arm to the trunk via the sternoclavicular joint and lists the SC, AC, scapulothoracic and glenohumeral joints. The exact 'pectoral' synonym was not in the retrieved snippet.

sentence: The head of the humerus, the top of the upper arm bone, meets the glenoid cavity of the scapula to form the shoulder joint.
evidence: StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: the joint unites the humeral head with the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

sentence: At the top of the humerus the smooth rounded head forms the ball of the shoulder joint.
evidence: Head of the humerus as the ball of the ball-and-socket joint is standard (StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint). 'Smooth rounded' is descriptive and was not separately retrieved.

sentence: The anatomical neck lies just below the head and separates it from the greater and lesser tubercles.
evidence: StatPearls Humerus: the anatomical neck divides the head of the humerus from the greater and lesser tubercles (residual epiphyseal plate).

sentence: The greater tubercle is on the outer side and the lesser tubercle at the front, and both give attachment to rotator cuff tendons.
evidence: StatPearls Rotator Cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis on the lesser tubercle. Outer (lateral) and front (anterior) positions are standard.

sentence: The intertubercular (bicipital) groove runs between the tubercles and holds the tendon of the long head of biceps.
evidence: StatPearls Humerus: the intertubercular groove lies between the tubercles and contains the tendon of the long head of biceps (with an ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery).

sentence: Below the tubercles the bone narrows at the surgical neck, where the expanded upper end meets the shaft, and fractures are common there.
evidence: StatPearls Humerus: the surgical neck is the constriction distal to the tuberosities and is the most frequently fractured part of the humerus, particularly in older adults.

sentence: The shoulder, or glenohumeral, joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint in which the rounded head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity of the scapula.
evidence: StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: ball-and-socket (structurally), diarthrodial multiaxial joint uniting the humeral head and glenoid cavity. OpenStax 9.6 names it the glenohumeral joint, a ball-and-socket synovial joint.

sentence: Ball-and-socket joints have the greatest range of motion of all synovial joints, and OpenStax notes that the shoulder has little in the way of ligament support.
evidence: OpenStax 9.4: the ball-and-socket joint allows the greatest range of motion. OpenStax 9.6: the glenohumeral joint has the largest range of motion of any joint; ligament support is only 'additional but weaker' (coracohumeral and glenohumeral ligaments) and the rotator cuff gives the primary support. 'Little in the way of ligament support' is a fair paraphrase but I could not confirm that exact phrase. Optional wording if the attribution is queried: '...and OpenStax describes the shoulder's ligaments as giving only additional, weaker support.'

sentence: This mobility comes at a cost in stability, because the glenoid is a shallow socket and the joint capsule is loose.
evidence: OpenStax 9.6: the shallow glenoid socket allows extensive range of motion and the capsule is 'relatively thin and loose to allow for large motions'; OpenStax frames the mobility versus stability trade-off (compare the hip with strong ligaments).

sentence: A rim of fibrocartilage called the glenoid labrum runs around the edge of the socket, deepening it and adding stability.
evidence: PMC reviews: the labrum is a fibrocartilage ring that deepens the glenoid and increases contact area. StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: the glenoid is shallow and the labrum is one of the static stabilisers. OpenStax 9.6: the labrum extends around the margin of the glenoid cavity.

sentence: Thickened bands within the capsule form the glenohumeral ligaments, which are the main static stabilisers of the joint.
evidence: Overstated. StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint lists six static stabilisers (bony anatomy, joint congruity, labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, capsule, negative intra-articular pressure) and does not single out the ligaments as the main one. OpenStax 9.6 describes the glenohumeral ligaments as 'additional but weaker' support and the rotator cuff as the primary support, and the preceding sentence already says the shoulder has little ligament support, so 'main' reads as inconsistent. Some reviews do call the capsulo-ligamentous elements the primary static restraints, so this is overstated rather than wrong.
suggested: Thickened bands within the capsule form the glenohumeral ligaments, which are among the static stabilisers of the joint, along with the labrum, the capsule and the shape of the bones.

sentence: Muscles add dynamic stability, mainly the rotator cuff; the long head of biceps arises from the top of the glenoid and labrum, and its stabilising role is debated.
evidence: OpenStax 9.6: rotator cuff muscles act as 'dynamic ligaments' and give the primary structural support. StatPearls (Proximal Biceps Tendinitis and related chapters): origin of the long head of biceps is established (supraglenoid region and superior labrum); its biomechanical role in dynamic stability is described as controversial, with several studies refuting an active stabilising effect.

sentence: The subacromial bursa lies beneath the acromion and deltoid and above the supraspinatus, which it protects from rubbing against the acromion.
evidence: Kenhub and PMC: the subacromial bursa sits between the deep surface of deltoid / acromion / coracoacromial ligament above and the supraspinatus and other cuff tendons below, and reduces friction between the tendon and the coracoacromial arch. OpenStax 9.6: the bursa prevents friction between cuff tendons and the scapula.

sentence: The rotator cuff tendons and this bursa pass through the space between the head of the humerus and the arch formed by the acromion, coracoid process and coracoacromial ligament.
evidence: PMC review: the subacromial space lies between the coracoacromial arch above and the humeral head / greater tuberosity below, and contains the cuff tendons, long head of biceps tendon, capsule and subacromial bursa. Arch = acromion + coracoid process with the coracoacromial ligament spanning them (standard; StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint calls the ligament a crucial part of the arch).

sentence: The rotator cuff is made up of four muscles, the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, often remembered by the letters SITS.
evidence: StatPearls Anatomy, Rotator Cuff: four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), mnemonic SITS.

sentence: Their tendons blend with the joint capsule to form a cuff around the joint.
evidence: StatPearls Anatomy, Rotator Cuff: the tendons blend with the joint capsule to form a cuff around the joint (anterior, superior and posterior; the inferior aspect is relatively unsupported). Kenhub: cuff tendons spread over and blend with the external surface of the capsule.

sentence: Supraspinatus helps to stabilise the joint and to start abduction, lifting the arm out to the side.
evidence: StatPearls Deltoid: supraspinatus is the primary abductor to about 15 degrees and deltoid takes over from 15 to 90 degrees. StatPearls Rotator Cuff: supraspinatus with deltoid initiates and continues abduction; the cuff muscles stabilise the humeral head.

sentence: Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate the arm outwards, while subscapularis rotates it inwards.
evidence: StatPearls Rotator Cuff: subscapularis is the primary internal (medial) rotator; infraspinatus and teres minor are the primary external (lateral) rotators.

sentence: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus, the axillary nerve supplies teres minor, and the upper and lower subscapular nerves supply subscapularis.
evidence: Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus (StatPearls Suprascapular Nerve); axillary nerve supplies teres minor (StatPearls Axillary Nerve, posterior branch); upper and lower subscapular nerves supply subscapularis (StatPearls Subscapularis: upper nerve the cranial half, lower nerve the caudal half; the lower nerve also supplies teres major, which the sentence does not claim).

sentence: The deltoid arises from the lateral part of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, and attaches to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.
evidence: StatPearls Deltoid: originates from the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula; inserts on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.

sentence: It has clavicular, acromial and spinal parts, is supplied by the axillary nerve, and its middle fibres abduct the arm.
evidence: StatPearls Deltoid: three parts (anterior, lateral, posterior), motor supply from the axillary nerve. Kenhub: clavicular, acromial and spinal parts; the acromial (middle) fibres are the main abductors.

sentence: The deltoid abducts the arm; its front fibres help flex it and its back fibres help extend it.
evidence: Kenhub Deltoid: anterior fibres flex and medially rotate, middle fibres abduct, posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate. Placement note only: this sentence sits under the 'Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints' heading but is about the deltoid; the content itself is correct.

sentence: The axillary nerve comes from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and passes through the quadrangular space beside the surgical neck of the humerus, together with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
evidence: StatPearls Axillary Nerve: arises from the posterior cord (C5, C6) and passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. StatPearls Quadrangular Space: boundaries are teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps and, laterally, the surgical neck of the humerus.

sentence: The suprascapular nerve comes from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and passes through the suprascapular notch.
evidence: StatPearls Suprascapular Nerve: arises from the upper trunk (C5, C6; C4 in some people), runs to the scapula and passes through the suprascapular notch into the supraspinatus fossa.

sentence: The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries arise from the axillary artery and together supply the shoulder joint, while the suprascapular artery supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
evidence: StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: supplied by the posterior and anterior circumflex humeral arteries, both branches of the axillary artery. StatPearls Scapula: the suprascapular artery mostly supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus (it comes from the thyrocervical trunk, which the sentence correctly does not attribute to the axillary artery). Optional nuance: the capsule also gets suprascapular and circumflex scapular branches.

sentence: The rotator cuff muscles stabilise the joint while the deltoid lifts the arm.
evidence: OpenStax 9.6: rotator cuff muscles ('dynamic ligaments') provide the primary structural support for the glenohumeral joint; StatPearls Deltoid: deltoid is the main abductor from about 15 to 90 degrees. Simplified (the cuff also rotates and supraspinatus starts abduction) but not wrong; the detail is in the rotator cuff sentences.

sentence: A dislocated shoulder means the upper arm bone has come out of its socket.
evidence: NHS Dislocated shoulder: a dislocated shoulder is when the upper arm bone comes out of place from the shoulder socket.

sentence: The NHS advises going to A&E if the arm cannot be moved, the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape, or it is painful, bruised or swollen.
evidence: NHS Dislocated shoulder: go to A&E if you cannot move the arm, the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape, or it is painful, bruised or swollen; ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance rather than driving yourself.

sentence: Treatment is usually a reduction in hospital, in which a clinician moves the bone back into place, followed by a sling.
evidence: NHS Dislocated shoulder: a doctor moves (rotates) the arm back into place, usually after an X-ray and with local anaesthetic or sedation, then a sling supports the arm.

sentence: The axillary nerve is the nerve most often injured in shoulder dislocation, causing weak lifting of the arm to the side and loss of feeling over the outer upper arm.
evidence: StatPearls Shoulder Dislocations Overview: the axillary nerve is the most frequently injured nerve; it supplies deltoid and teres minor and sensation over the lateral shoulder. StatPearls Axillary Nerve Injury: weak shoulder abduction (and external rotation) with numbness over the lateral upper arm ('regimental badge' area).

sentence: Most such nerve injuries recover, and numbness, pins and needles, or arm movement that does not improve needs medical review.
evidence: First clause is supported: StatPearls Axillary Nerve Injury says traumatic injuries after anterior dislocation or proximal humerus fracture recover without surgery in most patients; a PMC review says most are low grade, often fully recovering by about 12 weeks (worse outlook with a rotator cuff tear or tuberosity fracture). The second clause names no route to care ('needs medical review'). NHS Shoulder pain: ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for pins and needles that do not go away, numbness, inability to move the arm, or pain after a fall. NHS Broken arm or wrist: numbness or tingling after an arm injury means A&E or 999.
suggested: Most such nerve injuries recover without surgery, but numbness, pins and needles, or arm movement that is not improving should be checked: ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111, or go to A&E if it follows a new injury.

sentence: A fracture of the proximal humerus, the top of the upper arm bone, causes pain, swelling and difficulty moving the arm, and bruising can spread to the chest, elbow and forearm.
evidence: UK NHS trust proximal humerus fracture leaflets (Gateshead, St George's, Plymouth, UHCW, Leicester set): pain, swelling, bruising and reduced movement; bruising and swelling can spread to the chest, elbow and forearm. The single leaflet carrying the exact 'chest, elbow and forearm' wording was not individually identified.

sentence: Many of these fractures do not need surgery, and a sling is the usual first step.
evidence: StatPearls Proximal Humerus Fracture: minimally displaced fractures are the majority (about 50 to 65 percent); non-operative treatment succeeds in about 80 to 85 percent; non-operative care is a sling with progressive rehabilitation.

sentence: A suspected fracture needs assessment in A&E, and severe pain, numbness, pins and needles, or a cold, pale or blue hand needs urgent help.
evidence: The first clause (A&E) is right, but 'needs urgent help' names no route. NHS Broken arm or wrist: if an injured arm is numb, tingling or has pins and needles, or has changed colour or shape, go to A&E or call 999, and do not drive yourself. NHS Sprains and strains: skin that looks blue or grey or is cold means 999 or A&E. NHS children's arm-injury pages add pale or cold fingers.
suggested: A suspected fracture, especially with severe pain, needs assessment in A&E; if the arm or hand is also numb or tingling, has pins and needles, or looks pale, blue or grey or feels cold, go to A&E or call 999 straight away.

sentence: Rotator cuff problems range from irritation of the tendons, called tendinopathy or tendinitis, to partial or full-thickness tears.
evidence: StatPearls Rotator Cuff Syndrome: spectrum from tendonitis / tendinopathy and bursitis / impingement to partial- and full-thickness tears.

sentence: Tears can develop gradually over time or suddenly, for example after a fall.
evidence: StatPearls Rotator Cuff Syndrome: cause is multifactorial (degeneration, overuse, trauma); NHS trust rotator cuff tear leaflets describe both degenerative (gradual) tears and acute traumatic tears after an injury.

sentence: Rotator cuff tears can cause pain and weakness when lifting the arm, and night pain is common.
evidence: NHS trust and NHS Scotland rotator cuff tear leaflets: pain, weakness and reduced movement; night pain that disrupts sleep is common; some tears cause no symptoms. StatPearls: pain and weakness are the main presenting symptoms.

sentence: Most people start with non-surgical care such as physiotherapy, and surgery is considered for some tears.
evidence: StatPearls Rotator Cuff Syndrome: physical therapy is first-line and most patients without full-thickness tears improve without surgery. NHS Scotland and trust leaflets: exercise therapy first; surgery considered for traumatic tears or when non-surgical treatment has not helped.

sentence: Sudden arm weakness after an injury needs prompt medical assessment, and NHS 111 can advise which service to use.
evidence: Lower severity than S32 and S35. It names NHS 111 (consistent with NHS Shoulder pain: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if you cannot move the arm or have pain after a fall) but under-triages. NHS 111 Wales Stroke: face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech means phone 999 immediately; a Welsh health-centre page says call 999 for new weakness in the face, arm or leg, and A&E or 999 after a serious injury if the area has changed shape or cannot be moved. As worded, a reader with a possible stroke could be steered to NHS 111 instead of 999.
suggested: Sudden arm weakness after an injury needs prompt medical assessment: go to A&E if the arm cannot be moved or the shoulder looks out of shape, or ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111; call 999 if there is also a drooping face or slurred speech, which can be signs of a stroke.

sentence: Shoulder impingement is pain that arises when the rotator cuff tendons and subacromial bursa are compressed beneath the arch above the humeral head, and it typically hurts when the arm is lifted forwards or sideways.
evidence: NHS Shoulder impingement: pain in the shoulder, usually worse when you lift your arm. NHS 111 Wales: a swollen tendon rubs against nearby tissue or bone, causing pain on lifting the arm. PMC and trust leaflets: cuff tendons and subacromial bursa are compressed under the coracoacromial arch during elevation. 'Forwards or sideways' is standard textbook detail (some literature debates the mechanism).

sentence: In frozen shoulder the joint capsule tightens and becomes inflamed, causing pain and stiffness, often with night pain.
evidence: NHS and NHS 111 Wales: the capsule / tissue around the shoulder joint becomes inflamed and tight (thickened), causing pain and stiffness; pain can be worse at night and disturb sleep.

sentence: The cause is often unclear, but it is linked to diabetes, thyroid disorders and previous shoulder injury or surgery.
evidence: NHS inform and NHS trust frozen shoulder leaflets: cause often unclear; risk factors include diabetes, overactive or underactive thyroid, and previous shoulder injury or surgery (reduced movement). NHS 111 Wales: often not clear why; injury or surgery and diabetes are linked.

sentence: It passes through painful, stiff and recovering stages, and NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if shoulder pain does not improve.
evidence: NHS trust leaflets describe three phases (painful, stiff, recovery), but NHS inform Scotland says two stages and the NHS 111 Wales frozen shoulder page itself gives no stages (it says months or years, usually resolving). NHS 111 Wales: get help if shoulder pain and stiffness do not go away; NHS 111 Wales Shoulder pain: see a GP if not better after 2 weeks. Sentence is acceptable; if it is cited to NHS 111 Wales alone, the stages clause needs another source (or say 'usually described as passing through...').

sentence: Clavicle (collarbone), scapula (shoulder blade) and the upper end of the humerus (upper arm bone) on each side
evidence: Standard anatomy; StatPearls Shoulder and Appendicular Skeleton chapters cover clavicle, scapula and humerus.

sentence: Ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; ball-and-socket joints have the greatest range of motion of all synovial joints
evidence: OpenStax 9.4 and 9.6: shoulder = glenohumeral ball-and-socket synovial joint; ball-and-socket joints allow the greatest range of motion. StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: humeral head and glenoid cavity.

sentence: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis; their tendons blend with the joint capsule
evidence: StatPearls Anatomy, Rotator Cuff: four muscles (SITS) whose tendons blend with the capsule to form a cuff.

sentence: Axillary nerve, which supplies the deltoid and teres minor
evidence: StatPearls Shoulder Dislocations Overview: the axillary nerve is the most frequently injured nerve; it innervates deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the lateral shoulder.

sentence: Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries to the shoulder joint; clavicle: suprascapular, thoracoacromial and internal thoracic arteries; scapula: suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular arteries
evidence: StatPearls Glenohumeral Joint: anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries (branches of the axillary artery). StatPearls Clavicle: suprascapular, thoracoacromial and internal thoracic arteries. StatPearls Scapula: suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular arteries. Optional nuance: suprascapular and circumflex scapular branches also reach the joint capsule.

sentence: Clavicle fracture, acromioclavicular dislocation, shoulder dislocation and proximal humerus fracture
evidence: Standard list. StatPearls: AC joint injuries are a large share of shoulder injuries (over 40 percent in the cited series), anterior dislocation is up to 97 percent of shoulder dislocations, proximal humerus fractures are common; clavicle fracture is a standard common injury.
